exam: A 4‑year‑old presents with a left‑sided neck tilt, no fever, and a firm SCM – what is the most likely diagnosis and initial management? — Congenital muscular torticollis; start gentle stretching and physiotherapy, monitor growth.

A patient with HIV on ART develops painful right neck tilt, fever, and dysphagia. Which investigation is most urgent? — Neck CT with contrast to rule out retropharyngeal abscess; start empirical antibiotics.

You see a road‑traffic‑injury victim with fixed neck tilt, midline tenderness, and neurological weakness. What is your next step? — Immobilise cervical spine, obtain urgent X‑ray/CT, arrange neurosurgical review.

How does tuberculous spondylitis cause torticollis and what key sign helps differentiate it from simple muscle spasm? — Vertebral destruction leads to gibbus and chronic pain; presence of constitutional symptoms and ESR elevation points to TB.

Why is NSAID preferred over high‑dose steroids in acute spasmodic torticollis in a malaria‑endemic area? — NSAIDs provide analgesia without immunosuppression that could worsen undiagnosed malaria or TB.
A newborn has a firm, thickened SCM and limited neck rotation. What long‑term complication should you counsel parents about if untreated? — Persistent facial asymmetry and plagiocephaly.
Which red‑flag sign would prompt immediate airway protection in a patient with torticollis? — Stridor or rapidly worsening dyspnoea.

What physiotherapy technique is most effective for chronic congenital torticollis after 1 year of conservative care? — Manual stretching combined with positioning therapy; consider surgical release if no improvement.
ai.title: Torticollis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Torticollis is an abnormal, painful neck posture caused by muscle spasm or structural lesions. In low‑resource settings, infections, trauma and congenital causes are common. Prompt recognition and targeted investigation guide safe management.

b: Acute spasmodic torticollis – often idiopathic or post‑viral
Congenital muscular torticollis – SCM fibrosis in infants
Secondary torticollis – trauma, infection, tumour, cervical spine disease
sections.p: Torticollis describes a fixed lateral flexion of the neck with rotation to the opposite side. It may be acute (spasmodic) or chronic (congenital, post‑traumatic, neoplastic). The key clinical problem is restricted airway, pain and risk of neurologic compromise.

b: Head tilted toward the side of the tight sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and chin rotated opposite
Pain, limited range of motion, possible fever or neurological deficits
Red flag: progressive weakness, dysphagia, respiratory distress
sections.p: Diagnose by pattern of head tilt, associated signs and a focused history. Classify by duration (acute <2 weeks, chronic ≥2 weeks) and aetiology (muscular, osseous, neurologic).

b: Infection → rapid swelling, fever, neck pain, possible airway compromise
TB spondylitis → chronic pain, gibbus, constitutional symptoms
Trauma → vertebral fracture, ligament injury, may need imaging
sections.p: In East African hospitals, common causes include cervical lymphadenitis, retropharyngeal abscess, tuberculous spondylitis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections, and trauma from road‑traffic accidents.
When imaging is unavailable, rely on clinical red flags and treat presumptively for infection if fever and swelling are present.

t.b: Is there vertebral fracture, subluxation or bony abnormality? → Positive: fracture or dislocation; Negative: consider soft‑tissue cause
Is the SCM thickened or fibrotic? → Thickening supports congenital muscular torticollis
Is there an inflammatory or infectious process? → Elevated WBC/ESR suggests infection
Is immunosuppression present? → Positive guides need for opportunistic infection work‑up
Is there an abscess, tumour or spinal cord compression? → Positive directs surgical drainage or oncologic referral

b: Acute spasm – NSAID + gentle passive stretching; avoid high‑dose benzodiazepines in liver disease
Infection – empirical broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑cloxacillin) covering Staph aureus; add anti‑TB therapy if TB spondylitis suspected
Trauma – cervical immobilisation, analgesia, refer for orthopaedic review
Congenital – early physiotherapy, stretching; consider surgical release after 1 year if no improvement
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide analgesia, muscle relaxation and physiotherapy. Monitor airway and neurologic status closely.

b: Spasmodic dysphonia – voice change without neck deformity
Cervical dystonia (segmental) – involves multiple neck muscles, not just SCM
Atlanto‑axial subluxation – seen in rheumatoid arthritis, presents with instability rather than fixed tilt

sections.p: Normal X‑ray does not exclude deep‑space infection; ESR may be modest in early TB; HIV‑negative does not rule out opportunistic infection in early seroconversion.
